newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA welcomes new Superfund debate.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA welcomes new Superfund debate.

text.p: The Clinton administration welcomed a proposal Tuesday by Senate Republicans to overhaul the multibillion dollar Superfund toxic waste cleanup program, but at least one green group was quick to slam it.

"EPA looks forward to working with the 105th Congress to achieve the responsible bipartisan legislation we need to reform the nation's toxic waste cleanup law," an Environmental Protection Agency spokeswoman said.
Last month, senior administration officials had said there was no longer any need for sweeping Superfund legislation because EPA had found ways to cut costs and speed up cleanups.
"Any new reauthorization attempt should reflect and incorporate those reforms," EPA said in its latest statement.
Similar legislation was bogged down last year in a battle over who should cover cleanup costs at sites where companies and municipalities dumped waste legally before 1981.
The Environmental Defense Fund said the new proposal was seriously flawed.
"The bill rolls back liability for some industrial polluters," EDF senior attorney Karen Florini said.

The bill by Republican Senators John Chafee of Rhode Island and Bob Smith of New Hampshire would assign cleanup costs proportionally at sites where several companies dumped waste, instead of making one or a few of them pay all costs.
Chafee said the proposal would speed cleanups by setting decontamination standards based on the future use of the site, rather than holding all cleanups to the same strict standards.
But Florini said the bill "fails to protect groundwater as a valuable resource for future generations."
The Environmental Defense Fund also slammed the bill's plan to cap the number of sites which could be added to the Superfund program, saying it would undercut incentives for managing existing dumps.
"This could force states to have to deal with 1,400 to 2,300 additional sites, at costs of $8.4 to $19.9 billion," Florini said.
